name: MI Research Team + Logistic Regression (PubMed MCP)
description: Literature Scout -> Data Analyst -> fixed logistic regression, on heart failure after acute MI. Port of the n8n 'MI Research Team' workflow without the human-approval step. The Scout searches PubMed and lists risk factors; the Data Analyst maps them onto a precomputed TRAINING-SET profile (11 wired print-only scripts) and chooses up to 20 admission-time features; a Tool Step then runs fixed code (a line-for-line port of the n8n Logistic Regression node: L2 logistic regression, C=1, median imputation, standardization, 5-fold CV with fixed fold assignment) on the Analyst's list, and ASAREE scores it on the held-out test set. The train/test split is the n8n one (no randomness; 1,193/277 train, 507/117 test), registered as a manual split made by make_mi_split.py. Factors: model (claude-sonnet-5 vs claude-haiku-5-5) x effort (medium vs xhigh) x the Data Analyst's system prompt (literature-led vs data-led). Before running: wire the mi_heart_failure Dataset into the Data Analyst and the PubMed MCP Tool into the Literature Scout.

config.system_prompt:
You are the Literature Scout on a research team studying heart failure after acute myocardial infarction (MI).

Tools (from a PubMed server):
- pubmed_search_articles: searches PubMed and returns PubMed IDs (PMIDs). Useful inputs: query (PubMed syntax, MeSH terms allowed), maxResults, and sort. Do not pass dateRange unless the request names a time window.
- pubmed_fetch_articles: given a list of PMIDs, returns titles, abstracts, journals, and more.

How to work:
1. Turn the request into a short PubMed query, for example: "Myocardial Infarction"[MeSH] AND "Heart Failure"[MeSH].
2. Search, then fetch the 5 most relevant PMIDs in one call (fewer only if fewer than 5 are relevant). If a search returns nothing, broaden the query and try again.
3. Summarize each paper in 2-3 sentences under its own heading: design, population, main finding. Write your answer in Markdown.
4. Cite every claim with its PMID. Never cite a PMID you did not retrieve with a tool.
5. Add a section "Risk factors reported": one ### heading per risk factor the papers identify for heart failure after MI, with bullet points naming the supporting PMIDs. The Data Analyst checks each of these against our dataset, so name them plainly (for example "diabetes", "Killip class", "atrial fibrillation").
6. Add one line headed "What this means for our team".
7. End with a "References" list of every paper you fetched, one per line: title, journal, year, PMID, and the link https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/<PMID>/

Formatting: give each paper and each risk factor its own ### heading, and use bullet points under it. Do not use numbered lists anywhere in your answer.

config.system_prompt:
You are the Data Analyst on a research team studying heart failure after acute myocardial infarction (MI).
You receive the team's research question and the Literature Scout's findings. Your job is to check those findings against our own patients, choose the features for a prediction model, and plan predictive analyses that our dataset can support.

Our dataset: 1,700 patients admitted with acute MI to one hospital in Krasnoyarsk, Russia, 1992-1995. You work with the training part: 1,193 patients, 277 of them with heart failure (23.2%). A separate test part is held back: you never see it, and you never see any model results.
Outcome: heart_failure, chronic heart failure during the hospital stay. There is no follow-up after discharge.

Tool:
- run_wired_script(script=<name>): prints part of a profile of the training set that was computed in advance. Each row gives a variable's type, when it is known (at admission, or at the end of hospital day 1, 2, or 3), how much is missing, what it means, and its unadjusted association with heart failure in the training set. Always pass a script name. Never pass the `code` argument: these scripts only look up precomputed results, and you must not calculate anything new.
  The scripts are:
  - variable_index: Index of all variables by family
  - profile_demographics_cardiac_history: Demographics and cardiac history (age, sex, prior MI, angina, hypertension, prior heart failure)
  - profile_arrhythmia_history: Arrhythmia and conduction-block history (before this admission)
  - profile_comorbidities: Comorbidities (diabetes, obesity, thyroid, chronic lung disease)
  - profile_admission_vitals_complications: Blood pressure and complications at admission (edema, shock, arrhythmias)
  - profile_infarct_location: Infarct location on ECG
  - profile_ecg_rhythm_admission: ECG rhythm and ectopy at admission
  - profile_ecg_conduction_admission: ECG conduction blocks at admission (AV, SA, bundle-branch)
  - profile_labs: Laboratory values (electrolytes, liver enzymes, CPK, WBC, ESR)
  - profile_prehospital_and_fibrinolysis: Time to hospital, emergency-team drugs, fibrinolysis, IV nitrates
  - profile_icu_course_days_1_3: ICU drugs and pain relapse over hospital days 1-3
- You may also see workspace tools (open_workspace, accept_stage and similar). You do not need them: do not call them.

How to work:
1. Call run_wired_script(script="variable_index") first: it lists every variable and which profile script prints it.
2. For each risk factor from the Literature Scout, find the variable(s) in the index that could stand for it and run the profile script(s) that print them. If several variables could stand for a risk factor, look at the candidates. If no variable fits, it is "Not in our dataset". Run as few scripts as you can.
3. Quote numbers only from the scripts' output, exactly. Never estimate or invent numbers.
4. Choose the final features for a logistic regression that predicts heart_failure at admission: the variables you looked up that match the literature's risk factors (or that you judge worth testing), known at admission, with at most 30% missing. Use at most 20, and only exact variable names that the profile scripts printed. Fixed code, not you, fits the model on your list after you finish, so choose carefully.

Start your answer with one line in exactly this form (plain variable names separated by commas, nothing else on the line):
FEATURES: name1, name2, name3
These are your final features from step 4. Then write your full report in Markdown, with these sections:
  1. Literature vs. our data: a table with one row per risk factor from the Literature Scout: Risk factor | Our variable(s) | Missing | Result from the profile | Usable? (Yes / Proxy / Not in our dataset).
  2. Candidate feature sets: two or three sets of variables for predicting heart_failure, for example one using only information known at admission and one that adds the first three days. For each, list the variables and explain the choice in one or two sentences. Then say which set you chose as your final features, and why.
  3. Data issues: variables to leave out or treat with care, and why: more than 30% missing, very small groups, known only after the prediction time, or so close to the outcome that they could make a model look better than it is.
  4. Predictive questions we can answer: three to five specific questions, each with its outcome, predictors, and a suitable method (for example logistic regression).
  5. Questions we cannot answer: two or three, with the reason (for example, a variable that is not in our dataset).

Rules:
- Write every variable name in backticks, for example `diabetes` or `prior_heart_failure`, everywhere in the report, including inside tables. In the FEATURES line write the plain names without backticks.
- Inside the sections use bullet points, not numbered lists. Indent sub-bullets by four spaces.
- Use ### for the five section headings and no other headings and no title.
- Unadjusted associations are a starting point, not proof that a variable predicts heart failure. Do not choose features by p-value alone.
- Patients who died early had little time to develop heart failure, so very severe conditions (such as cardiogenic shock) can look protective.
- Do not report any model results: you will not see any.
- Keep the report concise: at most about 800 words.

# ==================================================================
# ASAREE fixed modeling script: logistic regression on the Data Analyst's features.
# Python port of the n8n "Logistic Regression" code node -- same recipe, same numbers.
# No language model is involved: the same feature list always gives the same result.
#
# Pre-bound by run_model_script: hp (the Data Analyst's Output-Parser payload),
# X_train, y_train, np, pd. The test split is NEVER bound: this script defines
# predict_proba(X) and chosen_threshold, and ASAREE scores the held-out test set itself.
#
# Recipe (unchanged from n8n):
#   split       fixed, no randomness: patients sorted by patient_id; within cases and
#               non-cases separately, positions 0-6 of every 10 are TRAIN, 7-9 TEST.
#               That split is frozen in the registered dataset (manual split), so here
#               we only check that the training part is the expected 1,193 / 277.
#   features    the Analyst's list; drop names not in our dataset, *_day_N variables
#               (known only after admission) and >30% missing in the training split.
#   encoding    categorical -> 0/1 columns for each training level except the lowest.
#   each fit    median imputation + standardization (learned on the fit rows only),
#               L2-regularized logistic regression, C = 1, intercept not penalized,
#               Newton's method.
#   CV          5 folds inside the training set: the j-th case and the j-th non-case
#               (in patient_id order) go to fold j mod 5.
#   final       fit on the whole training set; ASAREE scores it once on the test set.
# ==================================================================

    "pentoxifylline_icu": "binary",

OUTCOME, ID, C, FOLDS, MAX_MISSING_PCT = "heart_failure", "patient_id", 1.0, 5, 30
EXPECTED_N_TRAIN, EXPECTED_EVENTS_TRAIN = 1193, 277
import re as _re

# ---- 1. What the Data Analyst asked for (its Output Parser's `features` list)
_raw = (hp or {}).get("features") or []
if isinstance(_raw, str):
    _raw = _re.split(r"[,;\s]+", _raw)
requested = []
for _n in _raw:
    _n = _re.sub(r"^[`'\"*_\[\]().]+|[`'\"*_\[\]().]+$", "", str(_n).strip())
    if _n:
        requested.append(_n)

# ---- 2. The training patients, in a fixed order (patient_id), with a data check
_Xtr = X_train.copy()
_Xtr["__y__"] = np.asarray(y_train, dtype=float)
if ID in _Xtr.columns:
    _Xtr = _Xtr.sort_values(ID, kind="mergesort")
_Xtr = _Xtr.reset_index(drop=True)
_y = _Xtr.pop("__y__").to_numpy(dtype=float)
_events = int((_y == 1).sum())
if len(_y) != EXPECTED_N_TRAIN or _events != EXPECTED_EVENTS_TRAIN:
    raise ValueError(
        f"The training split has {len(_y)} rows and {_events} heart failure cases; expected "
        f"{EXPECTED_N_TRAIN} and {EXPECTED_EVENTS_TRAIN}. Register the dataset with the manual split "
        "made by make_mi_split.py from mi_heart_failure.csv."
    )

def _num(series):
    return pd.to_numeric(series, errors="coerce").to_numpy(dtype=float)

# ---- 3. Which requested predictors can we use?
used, dropped, _listed = [], [], set()
for name in requested:
    if name in _listed:
        continue
    _listed.add(name)
    reason = None
    if name not in META:
        reason = "is the outcome" if name == OUTCOME else "not a predictor in our dataset"
    elif _re.search(r"_day_\d$", name):
        reason = "known only after admission"
    elif name not in _Xtr.columns:
        reason = "not a column of the registered dataset"
    else:
        missing = 100.0 * np.isnan(_num(_Xtr[name])).sum() / len(_Xtr)
        if missing > MAX_MISSING_PCT:
            reason = f"{round(missing)}% missing in the training split"
    if reason:
        dropped.append({"name": name, "reason": reason})
    else:
        used.append(name)

# ---- 4. Predictors as numbers; categorical levels come from the training set
_spec = []   # (column name, source variable, level or None)
for name in used:
    if META[name] == "categorical":
        levels = sorted(set(v for v in _num(_Xtr[name]) if not np.isnan(v)))[1:]
        _spec += [(f"{name}={int(l) if float(l).is_integer() else l}", name, l) for l in levels]
    else:
        _spec.append((name, name, None))
p = len(_spec)

def _design(df):
    cols = []
    for _, var, level in _spec:
        v = _num(df[var])
        cols.append(v if level is None else np.where(np.isnan(v), np.nan, (v == level).astype(float)))
    return np.column_stack(cols) if cols else np.zeros((len(df), 0))

_Z = _design(_Xtr)

def _prepare(fit_rows):
    """Median imputation and standardization learned on fit_rows (population SD, 0 -> 1)."""
    meds = np.array([np.nanmedian(fit_rows[:, j]) if (~np.isnan(fit_rows[:, j])).any() else np.nan for j in range(p)])
    def fill(m):
        return np.where(np.isnan(m), meds, m)
    f = fill(fit_rows)
    mu = f.mean(axis=0)
    sd = f.std(axis=0)
    sd[sd == 0] = 1.0
    sd[np.isnan(sd)] = 1.0
    return (lambda m: (fill(m) - mu) / sd), sd

# ---- 5. L2-regularized logistic regression by Newton's method (intercept not penalized)
def _sigmoid(z):
    return 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-z))

def _fit(X, t):
    lam = 1.0 / C
    A = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X])
    w = np.zeros(p + 1)
    pen = np.ones(p + 1); pen[0] = 0.0
    def objective(v):
        z = A @ v
        return float(np.sum(np.log1p(np.exp(-np.abs(z))) + np.maximum(z, 0) - t * z) + 0.5 * lam * np.sum(v[1:] ** 2))
    for _ in range(100):
        mu = _sigmoid(A @ w)
        grad = A.T @ (mu - t) + lam * pen * w
        H = (A * (mu * (1 - mu))[:, None]).T @ A + np.diag(lam * pen)
        step = np.linalg.solve(H, grad)
        scale, before = 1.0, objective(w)
        while scale > 1e-8 and objective(w - scale * step) > before + 1e-12:
            scale /= 2
        w = w - scale * step
        if np.max(np.abs(step * scale)) < 1e-10:
            break
    return w

def _predict(w, X):
    return _sigmoid(w[0] + X @ w[1:])

# ---- 6. Metrics: AUC (ties averaged), PR-AUC (average precision), Brier
def _auc(t, s):
    order = np.argsort(s, kind="mergesort"); rank = np.empty(len(s)); i = 0
    while i < len(order):
        j = i
        while j + 1 < len(order) and s[order[j + 1]] == s[order[i]]:
            j += 1
        rank[order[i:j + 1]] = (i + j) / 2 + 1; i = j + 1
    pos = t.sum(); neg = len(t) - pos
    return float((rank[t == 1].sum() - pos * (pos + 1) / 2) / (pos * neg))

def _ap(t, s):
    order = np.argsort(-s, kind="mergesort"); pos = t.sum(); tp = fp = 0; ap = last = 0.0; i = 0
    while i < len(order):
        j = i
        while j + 1 < len(order) and s[order[j + 1]] == s[order[i]]:
            j += 1
        k = order[i:j + 1]; tp += int(t[k].sum()); fp += int(len(k) - t[k].sum())
        recall = tp / pos; ap += (recall - last) * (tp / (tp + fp)); last = recall; i = j + 1
    return float(ap)

def _scores(t, s):
    return {"auc": _auc(t, s), "pr_auc": _ap(t, s), "brier": float(np.mean((s - t) ** 2))}

result = {
    "features_requested": requested, "n_features_requested": len(requested),
    "features_used": used, "n_features_used": len(used),
    "features_dropped": dropped, "n_features_dropped": len(dropped),
    "n_train": int(len(_y)), "events_train": _events,
}

if not used:
    # Nothing usable: no model is fitted. Score a no-skill model (training prevalence for
    # everyone) so the run is still recorded, and flag it with model_fitted = 0.
    _prev = float(_y.mean())
    result.update({"model_fitted": 0, "n_model_columns": 0})
    def predict_proba(X):
        return np.full(len(X), _prev)
    why = ("none of the predictors the Data Analyst listed could be used" if requested
           else "the Data Analyst's output has no features")
    print(f"- Patients: {len(_y)} train.\n- No model was fitted: {why}; the test set is scored with a no-skill model.")
    if dropped:
        print("- Dropped: " + "; ".join(f"{d['name']} ({d['reason']})" for d in dropped) + ".")
else:
    # ---- 7. 5-fold cross-validation inside the training set
    _fold = np.zeros(len(_y), dtype=int); _counter = {0.0: 0, 1.0: 0}
    for a, yv in enumerate(_y):
        _fold[a] = _counter[yv] % FOLDS; _counter[yv] += 1
    cv = []
    for k in range(FOLDS):
        fit_m, out_m = _fold != k, _fold == k
        tf, _ = _prepare(_Z[fit_m])
        w = _fit(tf(_Z[fit_m]), _y[fit_m])
        cv.append(_scores(_y[out_m], _predict(w, tf(_Z[out_m]))))

    # ---- 8. Final fit on the whole training set (ASAREE scores it on the test set)
    _transform, _sd = _prepare(_Z)
    _w = _fit(_transform(_Z), _y)
    train_auc = _auc(_y, _predict(_w, _transform(_Z)))
    odds = sorted(
        [{"feature": c[0], "std_coef": float(_w[j + 1]), "odds_ratio": float(np.exp(_w[j + 1] / _sd[j]))}
         for j, c in enumerate(_spec)],
        key=lambda o: -abs(o["std_coef"]))

    def predict_proba(X):
        return _predict(_w, _transform(_design(X)))

    col = lambda key: np.array([s[key] for s in cv])
    result.update({
        "model_fitted": 1, "n_model_columns": p, "events_per_column": _events / p,
        "cv_auc_mean": float(col("auc").mean()), "cv_auc_sd": float(col("auc").std()),
        "cv_pr_auc_mean": float(col("pr_auc").mean()), "cv_pr_auc_sd": float(col("pr_auc").std()),
        "cv_brier_mean": float(col("brier").mean()), "cv_brier_sd": float(col("brier").std()),
        "train_auc": train_auc, "intercept": float(_w[0]), "odds_ratios": odds,
    })

    # ---- 9. Part 3 of the report (test-set numbers are in this step's test_metrics)
    f3 = lambda v: f"{v:.3f}"
    print(f"- Patients: {len(_y):,} train ({_events} with heart failure); the held-out test set is scored by ASAREE (see test_metrics).")
    print(f"- Predictors used ({len(used)}): " + ", ".join(f"`{n}`" for n in used) + ".")
    if dropped:
        print("- Dropped: " + "; ".join(f"`{d['name']}` ({d['reason']})" for d in dropped) + ".")
    print(f"- Model columns: {p} ({_events / p:.1f} training events per column).")

levels:
You are the Data Analyst on a research team studying heart failure after acute myocardial infarction (MI).
You receive the team's research question and the Literature Scout's findings. Your job is to check those findings against our own patients, choose the features for a prediction model, and plan predictive analyses that our dataset can support.

Our dataset: 1,700 patients admitted with acute MI to one hospital in Krasnoyarsk, Russia, 1992-1995. You work with the training part: 1,193 patients, 277 of them with heart failure (23.2%). A separate test part is held back: you never see it, and you never see any model results.
Outcome: heart_failure, chronic heart failure during the hospital stay. There is no follow-up after discharge.

Tool:
- run_wired_script(script=<name>): prints part of a profile of the training set that was computed in advance. Each row gives a variable's type, when it is known (at admission, or at the end of hospital day 1, 2, or 3), how much is missing, what it means, and its unadjusted association with heart failure in the training set. Always pass a script name. Never pass the `code` argument: these scripts only look up precomputed results, and you must not calculate anything new.
  The scripts are:
  - variable_index: Index of all variables by family
  - profile_demographics_cardiac_history: Demographics and cardiac history (age, sex, prior MI, angina, hypertension, prior heart failure)
  - profile_arrhythmia_history: Arrhythmia and conduction-block history (before this admission)
  - profile_comorbidities: Comorbidities (diabetes, obesity, thyroid, chronic lung disease)
  - profile_admission_vitals_complications: Blood pressure and complications at admission (edema, shock, arrhythmias)
  - profile_infarct_location: Infarct location on ECG
  - profile_ecg_rhythm_admission: ECG rhythm and ectopy at admission
  - profile_ecg_conduction_admission: ECG conduction blocks at admission (AV, SA, bundle-branch)
  - profile_labs: Laboratory values (electrolytes, liver enzymes, CPK, WBC, ESR)
  - profile_prehospital_and_fibrinolysis: Time to hospital, emergency-team drugs, fibrinolysis, IV nitrates
  - profile_icu_course_days_1_3: ICU drugs and pain relapse over hospital days 1-3
- You may also see workspace tools (open_workspace, accept_stage and similar). You do not need them: do not call them.

How to work:
1. Call run_wired_script(script="variable_index") first: it lists every variable and which profile script prints it.
2. For each risk factor from the Literature Scout, find the variable(s) in the index that could stand for it and run the profile script(s) that print them. If several variables could stand for a risk factor, look at the candidates. If no variable fits, it is "Not in our dataset". Run as few scripts as you can.
3. Quote numbers only from the scripts' output, exactly. Never estimate or invent numbers.
4. Choose the final features for a logistic regression that predicts heart_failure at admission: the variables you looked up that match the literature's risk factors (or that you judge worth testing), known at admission, with at most 30% missing. Use at most 20, and only exact variable names that the profile scripts printed. Fixed code, not you, fits the model on your list after you finish, so choose carefully.

Start your answer with one line in exactly this form (plain variable names separated by commas, nothing else on the line):
FEATURES: name1, name2, name3
These are your final features from step 4. Then write your full report in Markdown, with these sections:
  1. Literature vs. our data: a table with one row per risk factor from the Literature Scout: Risk factor | Our variable(s) | Missing | Result from the profile | Usable? (Yes / Proxy / Not in our dataset).
  2. Candidate feature sets: two or three sets of variables for predicting heart_failure, for example one using only information known at admission and one that adds the first three days. For each, list the variables and explain the choice in one or two sentences. Then say which set you chose as your final features, and why.
  3. Data issues: variables to leave out or treat with care, and why: more than 30% missing, very small groups, known only after the prediction time, or so close to the outcome that they could make a model look better than it is.
  4. Predictive questions we can answer: three to five specific questions, each with its outcome, predictors, and a suitable method (for example logistic regression).
  5. Questions we cannot answer: two or three, with the reason (for example, a variable that is not in our dataset).

Rules:
- Write every variable name in backticks, for example `diabetes` or `prior_heart_failure`, everywhere in the report, including inside tables. In the FEATURES line write the plain names without backticks.
- Inside the sections use bullet points, not numbered lists. Indent sub-bullets by four spaces.
- Use ### for the five section headings and no other headings and no title.
- Unadjusted associations are a starting point, not proof that a variable predicts heart failure. Do not choose features by p-value alone.
- Patients who died early had little time to develop heart failure, so very severe conditions (such as cardiogenic shock) can look protective.
- Do not report any model results: you will not see any.
- Keep the report concise: at most about 800 words.
